phase: Hays grass expansion Phase 2, diagnostic packet 6
scope_and_limitations: First five packets cover 40 unique names from all 57 staged candidates, confirmed before preparation.
Original Hays observations and review counts inherited; this pass verifies primary literature not photo pixels.
1999 Flora supplied directly observed descriptions when it actually treated the taxon; modern accepted splits and omitted taxa are not described as direct historical accounts.
Elymus macgregorii requires expert attention to transitional Texas specimens; northeastern key is comparative.
Avena sativa may be planted or casual cereal volunteer, not necessarily locally established.

sources: Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas 1999, Poaceae p.1334 (library PDF page 258)
Hagenbuch & Lemke 2015 Texas Hill Country grass study p.68

diagnostic_character_targets.description: Annual cereal grass about 40–100 cm tall in the regional Flora; crop or transient escaped volunteer is possible
Two narrow pointed leaf auricles are present but may wither early
Membranous ligule about 2–3 mm in regional treatment
Stiff, unbranched, two-sided terminal spike with sessile spikelets at opposite sides of a zigzag rachis
Spikelets typically 2–5-flowered, with lower two or three florets fertile
Broad asymmetric glumes at least around 3.6 mm wide, usually 3 or more veined, potentially awned or awnless
diagnostic_character_targets.required_same_specimen_photo: flattened glume with veins and ruler

taxa.prior_Hays_photo_summary: Distinct stiff, terminal wheatlike cereal spikes; some mature awned and some green heads, with full plant bases.
taxa.prior_Hays_photo_gaps: Wheat versus other Triticum, Hordeum or cereal cultivar forms cannot be established with certainty at this scale; observations may be crop or seed spill escapes rather than wild populations.
taxa.comparators: Hordeum vulgare, Secale cereale, Aegilops cylindrica and mixed seeded cereal grasses
taxa.next_same_specimen_evidence: Pair mature wheat spikelet and glume measurements with leaf collar and independently verify cultivated field/roadside spill versus reproducing wild Hays population.
taxa.risk_note: The old regional reference explicitly notes transient escape; authentic Hays occurrence is not equivalent to a naturally established population.

sources: Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas 1999, Avena genus (PDF 168)
Flora of North America, Avena sativa (republished Burke Herbarium https://burkeherbarium.org/imagecollection/taxon.php?Taxon=Avena+sativa)

diagnostic_character_targets.description: Cultivated or volunteer annual, often growing by roadside seed spill and erosion-control seedings
Open often drooping panicle with large pendulous oat spikelets
Usually 1–2 fertile florets in hulled oats, but substantially more in some naked-oat types; normal spikelets commonly 25–32 mm long
In cultivated oats, ripe florets generally stay attached to one another instead of easily breaking below each floret
Floret calluses generally glabrous or with very short hairs, unlike conspicuously bearded wild oat calluses
Lemmas typically awnless but sometimes carry weakly bent awns; absence of awns alone is not a species proof

taxa.prior_Hays_photo_summary: Pendulous oat-like spikelets and grass basal leaves; some field habitat.
taxa.prior_Hays_photo_gaps: Cultivated oats versus wild oats/forage mixtures and naturally established populations not determined.
taxa.comparators: Avena fatua, Avena sterilis, Avena strigosa; also cereal crop/forage mixtures
taxa.next_same_specimen_evidence: Examine mature spikelets and document whether florets stay attached to rachilla, the floret callus hairs, the glume lengths and awn structure; confirm whether plants were deliberately seeded.
taxa.risk_note: Cultivated and wild oats overlap; awn/no-awn is insufficient. The original reviewed Hays views provide only broad oat habit.

regional_flora.treated_name: Not treated under this name in 1999 Flora

sources: Flora of North America, Eragrostis minor (via Burke Herbarium https://burkeherbarium.org/imagecollection/taxon.php?Taxon=Eragrostis+minor)

diagnostic_character_targets.description: Usually low tufted annual grass, about 10–45 cm tall in FNA
Ligule short and ciliate, around 0.2–0.5 mm
Crater-shaped glands can appear on leaf margins, panicle pedicels and below culm nodes
diagnostic_character_targets.source: FNA via Burke Herbarium / Kew POWO

diagnostic_character_targets.description: Open to somewhat contracted panicle about 4–20 cm long with stiff divergent branches
Many-flowered compressed spikelets often around 4–7 mm long, generally about 7–12 florets in FNA sample; wider ranges occur
Small approximately 1.4–1.8 mm lemmas may carry glandular keel; paleas persist as lemmas detach upward along rachilla
diagnostic_character_targets.source: FNA via Burke Herbarium / Kew POWO

taxa.prior_Hays_photo_summary: Small weedy grass with open branched seedhead in disturbed bare ground.
taxa.prior_Hays_photo_gaps: Species identification requires mature glumes and lemmas, leaf glands/hairs, and precise spikelet measurement, not shown.
taxa.comparators: Eragrostis cilianensis, E. barrelieri, E. pilosa and other small lovegrasses
taxa.next_same_specimen_evidence: Show crateriform glands at pedicel/leaf margin with microscope macro, a measured ripe spikelet and retained paleas, plus the true ligule.
taxa.risk_note: Crateriform glands can be absent on individual structures; verify multiple characters. Old Hays photographs do not show these details.

sources: Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas 1999, Poaceae p.1236 (PDF p.160)

diagnostic_character_targets.description: Small annual often glabrous and blue-green, roughly 7–35 cm tall
Long membranous ligule about 3.5–7 mm
Dense slender cylindrical flowering head about 2–6 cm by 4–6 mm, technically a contracted panicle
Spikelets flattened from the side and single-flowered
Pair of conspicuously silky-haired glumes
diagnostic_character_targets.required_same_specimen_photo: macro of glume faces and margins

diagnostic_character_targets.description: Lemma awn roughly 3–5 mm arises from back near base and is bent near its middle
diagnostic_character_targets.required_same_specimen_photo: isolated lemma to locate awn origin

taxa.comparators: Phleum pratense, Polypogon spp., other foxtail-looking narrow grass heads
taxa.next_same_specimen_evidence: No original photo was accessible in the saved Hays sample; secure permissioned Hays specimen images documenting 1-flowered spikelet, silky glumes, bent dorsal awn, and 3.5–7 mm ligule.
taxa.risk_note: Zero accessible source photos; species-level Hays identification must not be implied from field-head resemblance or literature alone.

sources: Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas 1999, Poaceae p.1250 (PDF p.174)

diagnostic_character_targets.description: Mostly hairless annual up to about 50 cm tall
Relatively prominent ligule approximately 5–10 mm long
Open panicle with distinct individually dangling spikelets on fine, often kinked stalks
Usually triangular or tapered toward tip, roughly as broad as long, about 2–6 mm across
Roughly 3–8 florets per spikelet
Smaller and more triangular than broad, longer-than-wide spikelets of Briza maxima
diagnostic_character_targets.required_same_specimen_photo: side-by-side B. minor and B. maxima

taxa.prior_Hays_photo_summary: Small nearly triangular pendulous spikelets on fine pedicels and low annual grassy plant, compatible with little quaking grass.
taxa.prior_Hays_photo_gaps: No scaled multi-floret dissection or ligule measurements; only one Hays record.
taxa.comparators: Briza maxima, Briza media, and immature pendulous Melica spikelets
taxa.next_same_specimen_evidence: Count actual florets and capture a millimeter-scale profile of the triangular head and 5–10 mm ligule; independently confirm the single Hays observation.
taxa.risk_note: Only one Hays observation with three prior images; photo shape is suggestive, but no scaled dissection was performed.

sources: Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas 1999, historical Pennisetum ciliare account, printed p.1310 (PDF p.234)

diagnostic_character_targets.description: Tufted or spreading perennial forage grass introduced from Old World tropics
Dense cylindrical bristly inflorescence; looks like Setaria from a distance
Bristles roughly 4–10 mm long, basally fused into a small bur/involucre
diagnostic_character_targets.required_same_specimen_photo: detached entire bur and basal bristle union

diagnostic_character_targets.description: Mature bristles fall together with the spikelet as a unit
Unlike Cenchrus, Setaria typically drops spikelets separately above persistent bristles
Modern candidate accepted name Cenchrus ciliaris; old regional flora printed Pennisetum ciliare

taxa.prior_Hays_photo_summary: Dense cylindrical buffelgrass-like head with long bristles, collar and habitat views.
taxa.prior_Hays_photo_gaps: Fused bristle bases forming detachable bur, and comparison to Setaria are not conclusive.
taxa.comparators: Setaria parviflora, Setaria pumila, Pennisetum villosum and Cenchrus setaceus
taxa.next_same_specimen_evidence: On a collected mature specimen show the basal union of bristles and detachment as one bur, plus ligule and spikelet, contrasting Setaria.
taxa.risk_note: A cylindrical bristly head by itself proves no species. Invasive/introduced status is descriptive background, not a native-plant recommendation.

sources: Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas 1999, Sclerochloa dura treatment, printed p.1316 (PDF p.240)

diagnostic_character_targets.description: Very small prostrate to erect annual, typically 3–10 cm, sometimes 18 cm, mostly hairless
Membranous ligule about 1–2 mm
Compact dense often unilateral spike-like head around 1–3 cm, rarely 4.5 cm
Ripe spikelets about 6–11 mm with about 3–4 florets
Blunt-ended thick glumes and lemmas showing prominent nerves
Typically roadside/disturbed hard-ground early-season annual

taxa.prior_Hays_photo_summary: Small low grass with short dense one-sided green inflorescence spikes in disturbed ground.
taxa.prior_Hays_photo_gaps: No scale for multi-flowered spikelets, ligule or glume/lemma nerve count.
taxa.comparators: Poa annua, Catapodium rigidum, Puccinellia-like grasses and other small disturbed-ground annuals
taxa.next_same_specimen_evidence: Photograph one whole 3–10 cm plant with mm scale, true ligule, and a mature dissected spikelet showing 3–4 florets, stout glumes and strong nerves.
taxa.risk_note: Only two prior Hays images. Compact seedheads alone do not verify this uncommon local candidate.

regional_flora.treated_name: Not recognized as separate named species in older 1999 Flora; compare historical Elymus virginicus

sources: Native Plant Trust Go Botany Elymus key https://gobotany.nativeplanttrust.org/dkey/elymus/
Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas 1999 Elymus virginicus concept comparison only (PDF p.192)

diagnostic_character_targets.description: Modern Kew accepts a separate species from Elymus virginicus; names cannot be inferred from old regional Elymus virginicus account
In a published key E. macgregorii has mostly erect spikes with often 15–30 rachis nodes
diagnostic_character_targets.required_same_specimen_photo: entire spike with numbered rachis nodes

diagnostic_character_targets.description: E. macgregorii has broader flattened glumes (generally 0.7–2.3 mm), contrasting narrow bristle-like Elymus villosus glumes
E. virginicus in northeastern key commonly has 9–18 spike nodes, versus more nodes in E. macgregorii; geographic overlap warrants caution
E. macgregorii often has shorter auricles (0–2 mm) than E. virginicus (2–3 mm) in cited key
diagnostic_character_targets.required_same_specimen_photo: leaf auricle and collar on scale

diagnostic_character_targets.description: Glumes and lemmas may be pubescent in E. macgregorii versus often glabrous or subtly rough in E. virginicus

taxa.comparators: Elymus virginicus, E. villosus and E. curvatus, with particular concern for transitional Texas material
taxa.next_same_specimen_evidence: CRITICAL ZERO PHOTO SOURCE: locate a verified Hays voucher or an authorized high-resolution collection of an entire spike, rachis nodes, auricles and measured glumes; only then consider separating the key state.
taxa.risk_note: Kew accepts species and Texas nativity but this does NOT verify the lone Hays iNaturalist record. Northeastern key may be imperfect for transitional Texas populations; expert herbarium determination needed.
